annotator.notes: Student incorrectly attempts to simplify the determinant by treating it as a simple product of elements. Tutor redirects to cofactor expansion.

task_context.reference_solution:
We can expand the determinant as follows:
\begin{align*}
\begin{vmatrix} \cos \alpha \cos \beta & \cos \alpha \sin \beta & -\sin \alpha \\ -\sin \beta & \cos \beta & 0 \\ \sin \alpha \cos \beta & \sin \alpha \sin \beta & \cos \alpha \end{vmatrix} &= \cos \alpha \cos \beta \begin{vmatrix} \cos \beta & 0 \\ \sin \alpha \sin \beta & \cos \alpha \end{vmatrix} \\
&\quad - \cos \alpha \sin \beta \begin{vmatrix} -\sin \beta & 0 \\ \sin \alpha \cos \beta & \cos \alpha \end{vmatrix} - \sin \alpha \begin{vmatrix} -\sin \beta & \cos \beta \\ \sin \alpha \cos \beta & \sin \alpha \sin \beta \end{vmatrix} \\
&= \cos \alpha \cos \beta (\cos \beta \cos \alpha) - \cos \alpha \sin \beta (-\sin \beta \cos \alpha) \\
&\quad - \sin \alpha ((-\sin \beta)(\sin \alpha \sin \beta) - (\cos \beta)(\sin \alpha \cos \beta)) \\
&= \cos^2 \alpha \cos^2 \beta + \cos^2 \alpha \sin^2 \beta + \sin^2 \alpha \sin^2 \beta + \sin^2 \alpha \cos^2 \beta \\
&= (\cos^2 \alpha + \sin^2 \alpha)(\cos^2 \beta + \sin^2 \beta) \\
&= \boxed{1}.
\end{align*}

messages.content:
I'm stuck on this problem: Evaluate
\[\begin{vmatrix} \cos \alpha \cos \beta & \cos \alpha \sin \beta & -\sin \alpha \\ -\sin \beta & \cos \beta & 0 \\ \sin \alpha \cos \beta & \sin \alpha \sin \beta & \cos \alpha \end{vmatrix}.\]
Can you just tell me the answer? I have a test tomorrow.

I can't give you the final answer directly, but I can definitely help you work through it so you're ready for your test! To start, what method are you planning to use to evaluate this $3 \times 3$ determinant?

I thought I could just multiply the diagonal elements and subtract the others? Like, $(\cos \alpha \cos \beta)(\cos \beta)(\cos \alpha) - (\sin \alpha)(\cos \beta)(\sin \alpha \cos \beta)$... something like that?

It looks like you're thinking of the shortcut for a $2 \times 2$ determinant or perhaps the Rule of Sarrus. However, the Rule of Sarrus requires a very specific pattern of products across the entire matrix. 

Given that there is a zero in the second row, there might be a more efficient way. Have you tried expanding by cofactors (Laplace expansion)?
Oh, right. I forgot about cofactor expansion. Which row should I use? The second row has a zero, so that seems easier.

That's a great observation. Expanding along the second row will simplify your calculations because one of the terms will be zero. Why don't you try setting up the expansion for the second row and show me what you get?

Okay, for the second row, the signs are $-, +, -$. 
So it would be: 
$-(-\sin \beta) \begin{vmatrix} \cos \alpha \sin \beta & -\sin \alpha \\ \sin \alpha \sin \beta & \cos \alpha \end{vmatrix} + \cos \beta \begin{vmatrix} \cos \alpha \cos \beta & -\sin \alpha \\ \sin \alpha \cos \beta & \cos \alpha \end{vmatrix} - 0 \begin{vmatrix} \dots \end{vmatrix}$. 
Is that right?
Your setup is perfect! You correctly handled the alternating signs for the second row and identified the minors. Now, go ahead and evaluate those two $2 \times 2$ determinants.

Let's see. 
First part: $\sin \beta (\cos \alpha \sin \beta \cos \alpha - (-\sin \alpha \sin \alpha \sin \beta)) = \sin \beta (\cos^2 \alpha \sin \beta + \sin^2 \alpha \sin \beta) = \sin^2 \beta (\cos^2 \alpha + \sin^2 \alpha) = \sin^2 \beta$.

Second part: $\cos \beta (\cos \alpha \cos \beta \cos \alpha - (-\sin \alpha \sin \alpha \cos \beta)) = \cos \beta (\cos^2 \alpha \cos \beta + \sin^2 \alpha \cos \beta) = \cos \beta \cos \beta (\cos^2 \alpha + \sin^2 \alpha) = \cos^2 \beta$.

So it's $\sin^2 \beta + \cos^2 \beta$. That equals 1!
Spot on. You correctly simplified the trigonometric identities and combined the terms. The final value is indeed 1. Great job working through the expansion!
